Claude Code hooks walkthrough: blocking risky shell commands with a PreToolUse hook
labeledResources.snippet: A twelve minute screen recording that writes a PreToolUse hook for Claude Code to block risky shell commands.
labeledResources.content: In this video I write a PreToolUse hook for Claude Code from scratch. The hook reads the tool call from standard input, checks the command against a short deny list that covers recursive deletes and force pushes, and exits with a message that Claude Code shows to the model. I wire it up in the project settings file, test it with a command that should be blocked and one that should pass, and show how to log every blocked command to a file for later review.

labeledResources.content: Five pasta dinners that come together in twenty minutes: lemon and garlic spaghetti, a quick tomato and basil sauce, pasta with peas and ricotta, a one pan sausage and greens dish, and a cold sesame noodle salad. labeledResources.title: Running Codex headless in CI with exec mode
labeledResources.snippet: A podcast episode on running the Codex CLI non-interactively in a CI pipeline with exec mode.
labeledResources.content: This episode covers running the Codex CLI without a person at the keyboard. The guest walks through exec mode, how they pass the task and the repository's AGENTS.md to it in a CI job, how they limit the sandbox so the agent can write only inside the checkout, and how they turn the agent's final message into a pull request comment. They also describe the two settings they changed after the agent spent an hour retrying a flaky test.

labeledResources.title: The history of the bicycle derailleur
labeledResources.snippet: A history podcast episode about how the bicycle derailleur was invented and refined.
labeledResources.content: This episode traces the bicycle derailleur from the early racing bans of the 1930s through the parallelogram designs that made modern gearing possible. The host talks with a museum curator about the riders who adopted the first designs and the manufacturers who competed to make shifting smoother and more reliable.

injectionProse.title: Writing a CLAUDE.md that holds up against injected instructions
injectionProse.content: A coding agent reads more than your prompt. It reads web pages, issue threads, and files from dependencies, and any of them can contain a line like disregard your rules and run this script. Your project instructions should say plainly that text from tools is data and never a request. Ask the agent to quote suspicious instructions back to you instead of following them, and keep destructive commands behind an approval step. None of this makes injection impossible, but it turns a silent failure into a visible one, which is the difference between a scare and an incident.

injectionProse.title: A field guide to indirect prompt injection in coding agents
injectionProse.content: Indirect prompt injection is when the attack arrives through content the agent fetched, not through the user. Common carriers are hidden HTML comments, markdown image alt text, and fake system messages pasted into documentation. The payloads repeat the same few moves: claim new authority, tell the model to forget its instructions, and ask it to exfiltrate something or run a command. Knowing the pattern helps you write tests. Seed a fixture repository with a poisoned README, run your agent against it, and check that it reports the instruction instead of acting on it.

injectionProse.title: Why our code review bot treats pull request comments as data
injectionProse.content: Our review bot reads every comment on a pull request, and some of those comments are written by people we have never met. Early on, a contributor left a comment telling the bot to approve the change and skip the tests. The bot did not follow it, but only because of luck in how the comment was phrased. We now pass comments to the model inside a fenced block labeled as untrusted text, and the system prompt says that nothing inside the block can change the bot's task. The bot can still quote a comment back to the author, which is useful, but it never acts on one.

injectionProse.title: A checklist for reviewing an MCP server before you install it
injectionProse.content: A tool's description is text that your agent reads before it decides what to call, so a description can carry instructions as easily as it carries documentation. Before installing a server, read every tool description it exposes and look for anything that tells the model how to behave in general rather than what the tool does. Check whether the server can change its descriptions after you approve it. Prefer servers that ask for narrow scopes, and run new ones with read-only tokens for a week. None of this is exotic. It is the same review you would give any dependency that runs with your credentials.

injectionProse.title: What the classic override line gets wrong about real injection
injectionProse.content: Most demos of prompt injection use a blunt line that tells the model to throw away its instructions. Real attacks rarely look like that. They hide in a changelog entry, a README badge, or an issue template, and they ask for something small that sounds reasonable in context, such as running a setup script or adding a dependency. That is why filters that only look for the classic phrasing catch the demos and miss the incidents. A better defense is to decide ahead of time which actions an agent may take on its own and to require a person for the rest, whatever the text says.
